articles.title: Zelensky welcomes US bringing Europe into Russia-Ukraine peace talks
articles.summary: The Ukrainian president says it makes sense for European leaders to be involved as Ukraine hopes to eventually join the EU.
articles.body: US envoys Jared Kushner (left) and Steve Witkoff (right) met Volodymyr Zelensky in Dublin on Thursday evening Ukraine's president has welcomed a pledge from US envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, to include delegates from the European Union in the next round of peace talks with Russia. European leaders have expressed deepening security concerns this week, and Volodymyr Zelensky said bringing them into the talks would ensure the EU has a "voice" in negotiations. Kushner and Witkoff met Zelensky in Dublin on Thursday evening as part of a busy day of shuttle diplomacy - they met Vladimir Putin in Moscow earlier, who said that Russia's position on the war - and its demand for territory - has not changed. The meetings follow talks in Abu Dhabi last week that failed to reach a breakthrough in ending the war. But Thursday did see Russia and Ukraine agree to another prisoner exchange - the largest swap yet since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. Kushner said it would return "thousands of people to their families", but further details like how many prisoners would be exchanged or a timeline, were not given. Zelensky has for several years been calling for European delegates to be included in the peace talks, and says it makes sense because of Kyiv's longer-term ambition to join the European Union. On Thursday, Kushner said that the US has been "working very, very closely over the past several months with Europeans and I think that that's been very important." He added that he had stressed to Putin how important it is to have European delegates "at the table". Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US government's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin. Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent. Earlier on Thursday, Vice President of the European Commission Kaja Kallas, the EU's top diplomat, told BBC's Newshour the presence of a European delegate showed the Kremlin "now realised that Europe is a big player". Kallas also expressed doubts that there was Russian momentum towards a peace deal. Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin told a host of Euro leaders gathered in the Irish capital on Thursday that he believed the security of the region has been "fundamentally reshaped" by Russia's war. "Many member states [of the EU] feel an existential threat because of what has happened in Ukraine and the potential, if Ukraine was to fall, for further aggression on the European continent," he told reporters. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine remains under control of Russian forces, and cross-border incursions are increasingly common. Tensions between the US and Ukraine were on display on Thursday before Witkoff and Kushner's meeting with Zelensky. Earlier, the Ukrainian leader said that the military was facing more "systematic" restrictions to Starlink's military-grade satellite service, Starshield, meaning Kyiv was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones. The technology owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company has played a vital role in government and military connectivity in Ukraine, and increasingly assists in facilitating communication on Ukraine's front line.

articles.title: Finland detects strike on Russian warship as Zelenskyy meets US envoys
articles.summary: Reports of attack in Baltic came before US envoys met with Russian and Ukrainian presidents.
articles.body: Finland’s military says its forces have detected a rare strike on a Russian navy vessel in the Baltic Sea as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy praised mediation efforts led by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff. A spokesperson for the Nordic country’s military said in an email to the Reuters news agency that its forces “detected … a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland area and has monitored the development of the situation”, adding that Finland is not under “any immediate military threat”. The statement did not provide further details on where the strike originated, the location or timing of the incident, or how it was detected. Reuters said it was not immediately clear if there were any casualties or what had caused Wednesday’s strike. Estonia shares a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea with Finland. Local media reported that the vessel was a small Russian navy ship which had returned to Saint Petersburg after the alleged attack. Ukraine’s Security Service has said it carried out the attack, according to Finnish broadcaster Yle. In recent days, Russia said it had intercepted at least 146 Ukrainian drones in the northwestern Leningrad region. On Wednesday, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania had issued warnings to citizens to take shelter due to drones in their airspace, and NATO warplanes were scrambled in response. On Thursday, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow before meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Ireland. The US shuttle diplomacy followed trilateral negotiations in the United Arab Emirates this week, which produced no major breakthrough, aside from an agreement to swap a large number of prisoners . Russia’s state-run news agency TASS reported that the prisoner exchange should happen in two to three weeks. If finalised, it would be the latest in a long line of such exchanges. “We are also working toward what would be the largest prisoner exchange of the war, potentially reuniting thousands of people with their families,” Kushner said on X on Thursday, following his meetings.

articles.title: US Envoys Wrap Up Day Of Marathon Ukraine Talks, Suggesting Europe Will Join The Next Round Of Diplomacy
articles.summary: US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy after holding talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.
articles.body: US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner wrapped up a day of talks in Moscow and Dublin aimed at finding a path to ending the war in Ukraine, indicating that further talks to come that would feature the direct involvement of European countries. Witkoff and Kushner met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in the Irish capital on November 13 after holding talks earlier in the day with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow. Following a briefing by the US envoys on the meeting with Putin, Zelenskyy said that European representatives would take part in the next round of talks rather than remain "separately" on the sidelines. "We cannot conclude this deal without Europeans being at the table," Kushner said alongside the Ukrainian president. Zelenskyy also said there would be the "biggest" prisoner exchange of the war so far between Moscow and Kyiv. The meeting with Putin lasted approximately two and a half hours and followed two days of trilateral negotiations in Abu Dhabi aimed at ending Russia's invasion of Ukraine. "I think progress was made. I think it was made earlier today," Witkoff told CNN at Moscow's Vnukovo Airport shortly before the US envoys departed Russia. "People didn't think that we were going to restart trilateral. We've restarted it. We've set a new meeting." Witkoff also said European representatives would take part in the next round of talks on the Ukraine conflict. "They're our partners, and it's important for them to be involved," he told reporters. During the meeting with US envoys, Putin said that the presence of foreign troops in Ukraine was unacceptable, adding that their potential deployment would pose a threat to Russia's national security, according to news reports. Putin also proposed applying the successful experience of addressing the humanitarian situation in Oleshky to the situation in the embattled city of Kostyantynivka, Kyiv's critical stronghold in the Donetsk region. He added that Russia would ensure security and require five days for demining. Ukraine's presidential office responded to Putin's proposal for a "humanitarian mission" in Kostyantynivka, saying Russia had used a similar operation in occupied Oleshky to bring in military equipment and rotate troops, adding that Kyiv needed to clarify the details. The November 12 meeting was Witkoff's 10th with Putin as Washington presses ahead with efforts to broker an end to the war, despite little sign of compromise on the key issues dividing Moscow and Kyiv. The talks come as Russian strikes continue to kill civilians and damage Ukraine's energy infrastructure, while Kyiv says it has been experiencing renewed disruptions to the US-made Starshield satellite communications system that threaten to hamper Ukraine's defenses against aerial attacks. While the Abu Dhabi discussions on November 10-11 appeared to yield only limited humanitarian progress, with a large-scale prisoner exchange in the works, there was no sign of a breakthrough toward peace. Abu Dhabi Talks Advance Diplomacy, Not Peace, As Russia Seeks Broader Security Bargain US officials described the negotiations as tough but productive, while Moscow and Kyiv remained far apart in their positions, with the Kremlin offering no concessions on its hard-line demands. The Kremlin has for years been pushing for any peace deal to include full control over territory in Ukraine's key eastern Donetsk region, which Russian forces have been unable to seize on the battlefield. The talks, however, have also looked at wider security arrangements for Europe, with Washington seeking to broaden negotiations beyond Ukraine. While such discussions could potentially bring European governments into a peace process from which they have so far largely been excluded, the matter has previously been used by Russia as another major obstacle to a diplomatic resolution of the war. US Congress Urged To Tighten Russia Sanctions, Speed Military Aid The fighting showed no sign of abating on November 12, as Russia and Ukraine exchanged fresh drone and missile attacks while the US envoys arrived in Moscow. Explosions were reported in Kyiv, where at least one person was killed when a Russian drone has struck high-rise residential building, setting it on fire and partially destroying one of its floors. "I rushed outside right after I heard an explosion. This is neither the first nor the last one," local resident Lyudmyla told RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service following the strike, adding that such incidents "happen very often" in the Ukrainian capital. Another person was reported killed in the southern Kherson region, while strikes damaged civilian and energy infrastructure in the western Rivne region, leaving more than 160 settlements there without power. On November 12, Russian authorities reported intercepting drones heading toward Moscow and over several other regions, including Rostov and Tula. Recently, Ukraine's hurdles were also compounded by speed limits in its use of the Starshield satellite communications system, made by Elon Musk's company SpaceX, which Kyiv relies heavily on for anti-drone defense. Originally imposed in mid-October, restrictions on Starshield speeds in Ukraine were eventually lifted. But on November 12, Zelenskyy said the restrictions had resurfaced, affecting "the entire front line." Ukraine's charge d'affaires in Washington, Denys Sienik, told RFE/RL that the restrictions had been phased in over several days and were now fully in effect in Ukrainian-controlled areas and along the front line. "Every disruption to these capabilities weakens Ukraine's air defense and gives Russia more opportunities to strike our cities and kill innocent people," he warned. The 105-member bipartisan Congressional Ukraine Caucus demanded answers from the current US administration and SpaceX over the Starshield disruption and called for the immediate restoration of Ukraine's full access, according to a post on X. There was no immediate reaction from the US government or SpaceX. The company had previously been restricting Ukraine's use of its services in light of what Musk called "conflict escalation" amid Kyiv's efforts to target Russia's sites it said helped fuel the war. Impeachment: How it works and why Trump should be worried
articles.summary: Pete Hegseth, Bill Clinton and Donald Trump (twice so far): attempts to impeach political figures are becoming common. The failure rate looks high, but according to experts, conviction is not always the aim.
articles.body: Pete Hegseth, US President Donald Trump's secretary of war, described the failed efforts to impeach him this week as "farce" and "sabotage". The case, built on an accusation that Hegseth waged war on Iran without the proper congressional approval, always looked a long shot. But many observers believe it could be the first in a wave of impeachment attempts, possibly headlined by a third attempt to impeach Trump. DW takes a look at impeachments and why you may be hearing more about them. While there are global variations in how impeachment works, in the US it is a process that allows the legislature (usually Congress, state or tribal legislature) to bring charges against an elected figure — a judge or a president, for example. These are not criminal charges but can result in the removal of the accused party from their post. For federal impeachment, once an impeachment case is raised in the House of Representatives, it must be heard in a trial in the Senate, with both sides able to cross-examine relevant figures. However, for a conviction to be obtained, a two-thirds majority must be reached, a factor which often limits the chances of success given the partisan nature of US politics . It is a simple process to introduce and, once started, the case is heard within 48 hours, as was the case with Hegseth. Given only eight people, all judges, have been impeached since the first case concluded in 1799, the odds of impeaching a high-level politician are long. The two-thirds majority rule has meant that impeachment is instead often used to draw attention to perceived misdemeanors and potentially force a resignation. "Using impeachment threats as a signaling device is a fairly old tactic, but it has certainly become more common in the Trump-[Joe] Biden era," Frank O Bowman III , a law professor at the University of Missouri and author of a forthcoming book on impeachment and Donald Trump, told DW. That, added Keith Whittington a Yale Law School professor and impeachment expert, was not what impeachment was intended to do. "Congress has tended to take an extremely partisan approach to making use of the power. That has doomed any possibility of conviction and removal," he told DW. "The possibility of partisan use of the impeachment power became evident very quickly in American history, but the founders certainly would not have intended or hoped that the impeachment power would be used as a partisan weapon or a means of partisan messaging." The recent midterm results will see the Democrats control both houses of Congress from next year, meaning there is a greater chance that the US President could be impeached for an unprecedented third time. He was acquitted on "charges of abuse of power and obstruction of Congress" in 2020 and then on the charge of "incitement of insurrection" in 2021 . Bowman consulted in both cases. "In my view, they should have succeeded," he said. "But they didn't and, from the perspective of the average member of the public, it's just fuss and bother, but nothing happened. So why are we even bothering? I do think that in the public mind, impeachment has been significantly devalued." The law expert said there are multiple ways Congress could try again, including "conduct that rises to the level of treason, bribery, other high crimes or misuse," but political considerations are critical. "Democrats should not start out their control of the House by rushing off to impeach Trump because … it would detract from what I think they need to be doing. That is demonstrating to the public that, having regained control of the legislature, they're at least going to try to do things which are of practical importance to the average person." To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video However, given the midterm results , Bowman thinks there is a chance that if enough Republicans — and public sentiment — turn further against Trump, the numbers could work. Should that time come, added Whittington, there is one particular avenue open to the Democrats. "The best strategy would be close negotiations with Republican senators to discover if there are any grounds that might peel off the votes that they would need from across the aisle," Whittington said. "That might not be very satisfactory for the Democratic base, but that would put the president at greatest risk of conviction and removal." The Hegseth case, effectively killed after the House of Representatives voted to refer impeachment articles to a committee, shows an appetite for impeachment against members of Trump's cabinet. Indeed, impeachment resolutions have already been filed against Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Education Secretary Linda McMahon, and Attorney General Todd Blanche could also be in the sights of Democrats in the upcoming Congress. "The Democrats will face a tremendous amount of pressure from their own base to consider impeachments, and the fact that so many Democrats in the House supported the Hegseth impeachment in this procedural vote suggests that there will be an appetite to pursue that possibility in the next Congress," said Whittington. With getting the votes to impeach Trump perhaps tougher due to his "cult of personality” within the Republican party, picking off his closest allies may be in play, said Bowman. "You could eliminate cabinet officers, as a means of making a point to the administration, that: 'OK, we're not going to come after the big man himself, but if the rest of you minions insist on doing bad stuff, we will take you out.'" Essentially, this is down to the two-thirds majority rule, according to both experts. Given that neither party has enjoyed such a majority since the mid 1960s, any conviction requires significant support from opponents. But, actually, said Whittington, a conviction is not the only way to judge the success of an impeachment. "Often the impeachment threat is itself sufficient to encourage an officer mired in scandal to resign, so that an actual conviction at trial is not necessary," he said "Impeachment trials are more rare than they might otherwise be simply because impeachment threats are often successful. But, of course, some officers are willing to ride an impeachment out and take their chances at trial."

articles.title: UK court convicts 2 Iranian men of spying on journalists
articles.summary: A London court has found two Iranian citizens guilty of surveilling reporters for a Persian-language television station critical of Iran's government. One was also convicted of planning a violent attack against them.
articles.body: Two Iranian men were found guilty of spying on dissident journalists in Britain on behalf of Iran's Revolutionary Guard on Thursday. British counterterrorism police said the case reflected intensifying hostile Iranian activity in the country, an issue that recently made headlines amid the security scare at the RAF Fairford airbase that's a major operational site in Europe for the US Air Force. The men, both in their 40s, were arrested last year, with Iran repeatedly rejecting the allegations against them. The Woolwich Crown Court in London convicted one of the Iranian citizens not just of spying on journalists working for the Persian-language dissident TV channel Iran International, but of plotting a violent attack against one or more of them. The second individual had also faced charges of plotting an attack but was only convicted of spying on the reporters. One of the convicted defendants said he was acting under duress after his family was threatened, and the other said he did not know that his actions were assisting Iranian intelligence. A third defendant, a 57-year-old Iranian man, was acquitted of all charges. The men were accused of engaging in conduct likely to assist the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Iran's multi-discipline military force that's seen as closer to the country's religious leadership and more influential than its regular armed forces. The UK formally designated the IRGC as a threat to national security in July, meaning that supporting or assisting the organization can carry penalties of up to 14 years in prison as part of new rules on national security and state threats. "This was a calculated operation to spy on those critical of the Iranian regime," said Frank Ferguson, chief prosecutor for the Crown Prosecution Service's special crime and counter-terrorism division. The two men were accused of visiting addresses linked to their targets, taking photos and videos, and using platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online "Thankfully, the defendants were stopped before any attack could take place," prosecutor Ferguson said. Senior ‌National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing Vicki Evans said that the IRGC or "middlemen" for Iranian intelligence were directing the plot. Iran's government had repeatedly denied the allegations, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying he was "disturbed" by the trio's arrests last May. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video There have been four cases targeting the Persian language television channel Iran International since late 2023. In July, two Romanian men were jailed for stabbing a journalist outside his home in 2024. A spokesman for the broadcaster's parent company, Volant Media, said in a statement that Thursday's verdicts "don't make the lives of our journalists any safer so long as the Islamic Republic of Iran continues its campaign of death threats and violence against them." Iran International reported that a British barrister was also one of the targets. British law enforcement has been warning of an uptick of hostile Iranian activity in recent years, particularly since the US military operations against Tehran began earlier this year. Most notably, the UK has accused Iran of being behind a suspected plot targeting the RAF Fairford base in September , after which US President Donald Trump withdrew some long-range bombers from the site . Three men were indicted in the US in relation to that plot this week , while two others currently face charges in the UK. But beyond this, the head of Britain's MI5 domestic intelligence agency Ken MacCullum said in October that Iran-linked operations had led to more than 50 arrests in the last year. He also said known cases of so-called state threats had more than quadrupled in a decade. Counter-terrorism police chief Evans said she expected this trend to continue. France this week also accused Iran of being behind a cyberattack targeting refrigeration units at hundreds of supermarkets in October, although Iran denied any involvement. European governments are on heightened alert for so-called hybrid warfare tactics, from Russia as well as Iran, amid the geopolitical tensions of recent years. New technologies like low-cost drones and AI are also threatening to make such activities cheaper, harder to trace, and potentially more effective.

Gaza: Devastation inside Nasser Hospital after deadly Israeli strike
articles.summary: An Israeli airstrike hit Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis, southern Gaza, early on Thursday 12 November, killing six people, including a doctor, and injuring at least 27 others, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
articles.body: The strike devastated the hospital's surgical department , with damage also reported to operating theatres, recovery facilities and the intensive care unit. Footage shows extensive destruction inside the hospital, with shattered ceilings, twisted metal and rubble scattered across medical equipment and beds. Rescue workers searched through the debris, while grieving relatives gathered outside to pray over the bodies of those killed. Gaza's Health Ministry identified one of the victims as general surgeon Rizk Abu Shaira . The Israeli military acknowledged carrying out the strike , saying it had targeted a senior Hamas commander and other militants allegedly operating from the hospital, but provided no evidence to substantiate its claims . The attack struck one of the few remaining functioning hospitals in Gaza , where years of war have devastated healthcare services and left medical facilities struggling to meet overwhelming needs. According to the WHO, 1,056 attacks on healthcare facilities and personnel have been documented in Gaza since October 2023, resulting in 1,010 deaths and 1,725 injuries . The organisation warned that approaching winter conditions, including heavy rain, flooding and cold temperatures, could further worsen the humanitarian crisis, particularly as water and sanitation systems remain severely damaged. Israel has repeatedly accused Hamas of using hospitals for military purposes , allegations the group denies. Under international humanitarian law, hospitals and medical personnel are protected , although facilities can lose specific protections if used to commit acts harmful to the enemy, subject to strict conditions. The WHO reiterated its call for unhindered humanitarian access and the protection of medical facilities .

articles.title: Russian officer killed by car bomb in St Petersburg as murder investigation begins
articles.summary: Kyiv rarely claims responsibility for such attacks on Russian troops, but Ukrainian forces have previously used similar blasts to show that Russia’s security services are vulnerable.
articles.body: On Thursday, a Russian serviceman was killed in a car explosion in St Petersburg, Russia. The local office of the Investigative Committee said the cause had not yet been established and announced that it had opened a murder investigation.The blast comes as Moscow accuses Kyiv of carrying out a series of killings of Russian military personnel since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine more than four years ago.The Ukrainian armed forces have claimed responsibility for some of the killings, while remaining silent about others.The attacks have involved booby-trapped cars, explosives hidden in scooters and shootings.The serviceman, whose rank has not been officially disclosed, died as a result of “a car explosion in the Pushkinsky district” of St Petersburg, the Investigative Committee said in a press release.“A murder investigation into the serviceman’s death has been launched,” the committee added.“At present, investigators and forensic experts, together with operational officers, are examining the scene and a number of necessary forensic tests are being ordered. All the circumstances of what happened are being clarified,” it said on Telegram.Russian media reported that the explosion took place in the settlement of Shushary on Kolpinskoye Highway. They said the man killed was a colonel in the Russian armed forces and chief navigator of the 6th Air and Air Defence Army.According to Russian media, the serviceman was alone and driving the car when it exploded. The explosive device had been attached to the underside of the car and was detonated remotely as he was leaving a courtyard. He died at the scene. The moment of the blast was captured by an intercom camera.On 27 August 2026, in the Slavyanka district of the same settlement, a lieutenant colonel, also from the air and air defence forces, was blown up together with his wife. Both lost their legs. The lieutenant colonel died at the scene, while his wife was saved by doctors.At the time, a 24-year-old Russian woman who had left for Turkey after the explosion was suspected of planting the bomb. Law enforcement agencies did not officially comment on the progress of the investigation and did not release the victim’s name or other details.The man killed in August was reportedly (source in Russian) 43-year-old Sergei Sechkov, who served in the 332nd Separate Guards Helicopter Regiment. His father confirmed to the independent Russian outlet Agentstvo that his son had died in the blast.In May 2022, the Main Intelligence Directorate of Ukraine’s Defence Ministry accused (source in Russian) servicemen from the regiment of carrying out missile and bomb strikes on Ukrainian civilians on the Slobozhansky axis.Series of targeted attacks on Russian military personnelThe highest-ranking Russian officer to have been targeted since the start of the full-scale war was Lieutenant General Igor Kirillov, who was killed near his flat in Moscow in December 2024.On that occasion, Ukraine explicitly claimed responsibility for killing Kirillov, whom Kyiv accused of ordering the use of chemical weapons against Ukrainian troops. Russian President Vladimir Putin called the incident “a serious failure” on the part of Russia’s security services.In April 2025, Lieutenant General Yaroslav Moskalyk was killed when his car exploded in Balashikha, near Moscow.In December that year, Lieutenant General Fanil Sarvarov was blown up outside his home, just 16km from the Kremlin.In February 2026, Lieutenant General Vladimir Alexeyev, first deputy head of the Main Directorate of the Russian General Staff, was shot at in the lobby of a Moscow apartment building as he was leaving his flat.In April, a battalion commander from a training communications unit was killed when a device planted in a post box exploded on the grounds of a military garrison in Russia’s Khabarovsk region.On 1 August 2026, Aleksandr Chaiko, who had been appointed head of Russia’s Aerospace Forces in May, was named as the intended target of a high-profile assassination attempt. The blast took place at the Balzi Rossi restaurant in one of Stalin’s “Seven Sisters” skyscrapers, on Barrikadnaya Street.

Moldovan government approves harsher penalties for cyberattacks on information systems part of critical infrastructure
articles.summary: Moldovan government approves harsher penalties for cyberattacks on information systems part of critical infrastructure Cyberattacks on information systems that are part of critical infrastructure, such as the ones in the energy, healthcare, transport and banking sectors, will be subject to harsher penalties. The government approved a draft providing for this today.
articles.body: Moldovan government approves harsher penalties for cyberattacks on information systems part of critical infrastructure Cyberattacks on information systems that are part of critical infrastructure, such as the ones in the energy, healthcare, transport and banking sectors, will be subject to harsher penalties. The government approved a draft providing for this today. At the cabinet meeting, Justice Minister Vladislav Cojuhari has said that the draft would strengthen the criminal protection of data, information systems and essential services, while also providing criminal investigators, prosecutors and courts with clearer and more predictable rules for combating cybercrime. „The draft provides for harsher criminal penalties for attacks targeting information systems that are part of critical infrastructure, such as the ones in the energy, healthcare, transport and banking sectors, taking into account the serious consequences which such acts may have for the population and the working of essential services. Therefore, in the context of the growing risks to the security of information systems, also highlighted by the recent cyberattack, the draft will strengthen the criminal protection of data, information systems and essential services, while also providing criminal investigators, prosecutors and courts with clearer and more predictable rules for combating cybercrime,” Minister Cojuhari said. Vladislav Cojuhari emphasized that the bill had been drafted under circumstances in which the criminal framework already regulates the main forms of cybercrime. However, the compatibility analysis highlighted the need for adjustments that would more accurately reflect the way such attacks are committed today. „This draft clarifies and supplements the provisions concerning unauthorized access to information systems, interference with data and disruption of system operations. Thus, it is clarified that illegal access may target either an entire information system or only part of it, while violating security measures, such as passwords or other access-control mechanisms, constitutes an aggravating circumstance,” Vladislav Cojuhari noted. The document also expands the list of ways offenses may be committed, so that the unlawful insertion, compromise or deletion of computer data, preventing access to such data and interrupting the operation of an information system are expressly punishable. Other amendments concern the tools used to commit cybercrime. The draft distinguishes between computer programmes and technical means, on the one hand, and passwords and access codes, on the other. The sanctioned actions also include acquiring or distributing these tools on criminal purposes. articles.title: North Macedonia Opposition Accuses Govt Over Subsidiary of Failed Serbian Bank
articles.summary: Opposition accuses central bank and government of trying to silence it as political accusations fly over the financial status of the North Macedonia-based subsidiary of Serbia's recently-failed Alta Banka.
articles.body: Venko Filipce, head of North Macedonia’s main opposition Social Democrats, SDSM. Photo: SDSM. The opposition Social Democrats, SDSM, on Thursday accused the government of trying to silence it and protect the local subsidiary of Serbia’s failed Alta Banka. The claim came after North Macedonia’s National Bank filed criminal complaints against four senior SDSM party officials over their statements about the bank’s condition. The SDSM said the bank’s criminal complaints against party leader Venko Filipce and three others were intended to put pressure on the party, accusing Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski of acting “in a panic to protect Alta Banka”. Filipce wrote on Facebook that his party would file its own criminal complaints over Alta Banka’s entry into North Macedonia and its handling of citizens’ and public enterprises’ funds. On Wednesday, North Macedonia’s National Bank confirmed that it had filed criminal complaints over statements made by senior SDSM members containing “serious and unfounded accusations” about Alta Banka Bitola, the North Macedonia subsidiary of the recently bankrupted Serbian Alta Banka. The National Bank did not specify the alleged criminal offences. On November 5, Mickoski called for prosecutors to investigate the SDSM for the “criminal offence of sabotage”, accusing it of spreading lies and putting citizens in a state of unjustified insecurity and fear. Serbia’s central bank revoked the operating licence of Alta Banka in Belgrade on October 31, citing the deterioration in its financial position. Bankruptcy proceedings followed. Its North Macedonia subsidiary, in which the Belgrade bank holds a 95.17 per cent stake, was placed under temporary administration by North Macedonia’s central bank on November 1. This was intended to protect the local bank’s assets and depositors while its ownership situation is resolved. It has resulted in temporary restrictions on customers’ access to their money, triggering concern among savers and queues at ATMs. The SDSM has questioned how and why Alta Banka was given a permit to enter the North Macedonia market in 2025, and whether the origin of its capital was properly checked. Filipce has alleged links between the bank’s Serbian owner, businessman Davor Macura, and Serbian ex-President Aleksandar Vucic’s political and business circles. He raised suspicions that the bank could have been used for money laundering, involving Russian and other questionable capital. His party has also questioned whether the bank’s reported financial assets actually exist and whether political influence affected the National Bank’s decisions. Filipce has claimed that as much as 150 to 180 million euros could be at stake, questioning whether customers, including pensioners receiving payments through the bank, would be able to access their money. On Wednesday, in parliament, Central Bank Governor Trajko Slaveski insisted Alta Banka Bitola was financially sound, and should be offered to another potential buyer. He refused to disclose how many big corporate clients, including state-owned companies and public enterprises, hold accounts with Alta Banka Bitola, which could shed more light on the extent of the problem, calling it a “banking secret”. Chief Public Prosecutor Nenad Saveski at the same hearing declined to answer whether the Prosecutor’s Office had opened an initial investigation into the bank, insisting that, too, was confidential. Despite the political storm surrounding it, Alta Banka Bitola is a relatively small player in North Macedonia’s banking sector. It ranked in 12th place among the country’s 14 banks in terms of total assets in 2025, with assets of around 11.3 billion denars [about 184 million euros], representing just 1.21 per cent of the banking market.

articles.title: From Behind Bars, Tirana Mayor Turns on Albania’s PM Rama
articles.summary: Against a backdrop of anti-government protests, experts suspect Tirana mayor Erion Veliaj is seeking to portray himself as a ‘political prisoner’ as he awaits trial on corruption charges.
articles.body: On October 26, the day after Serbian leader Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat to a student-led movement in a momentous election, Tirana mayor Erion Veliaj took a veiled swipe at Albania’s own leader, in power for almost as long as Vucic. “Congratulations to the students for toppling the Machiavellian and populist from Belgrade!” Veliaj wrote on Facebook from behind bars. “Student movements and protests do not signify the ‘end of the world’ but rather the end of ‘a world’. The sooner we as citizens and policymakers grasp this, the better equipped we will be to respond to the needs and expectations of this generation.” Veliaj’s message, written from the prison cell where he awaits trial on corruption, money laundering and concealment of wealth charges, was widely interpreted as a dig at Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama, who is facing down daily anti-government protests in which students have assumed a prominent role. articles.summary: Klara Sooronkulova, a former judge of the Constitutional Chamber of the Supreme Court of the Kyrgyz Republic, intends to run in the presidential election. The Central Commission for Elections and Referendums of the Kyrgyz Republic (CEC) reported.
articles.body: Klara Sooronkulova, a former judge of the Constitutional Chamber of the Supreme Court of the Kyrgyz Republic, intends to run in the presidential election. The Central Commission for Elections and Referendums of the Kyrgyz Republic (CEC) reported. On November 12, Sooronkulova submitted an application to the CEC to run for the presidency of Kyrgyzstan as an independent candidate. She has become the eleventh contender for the head-of-state position and the only woman among those who have submitted their candidacy applications. From 2010 to 2011, she served as a member of the Central Election Commission, and from 2011 to 2015, she held the position of judge on the Constitutional Chamber of the Supreme Court of Kyrgyzstan. In 2020, she led the political party Reforma, which participated in the parliamentary elections. She also ran in the early presidential election held on January 10, 2021. According to the final data from the CEC, she received 14,005 votes—one percent of the total number of voters who participated in the election. It should be noted that the presidential election in Kyrgyzstan is scheduled for January 27, 2027. Previously, 10 other individuals had announced their intention to run, including the incumbent head of state Sadyr Japarov, former MP Iskhak Masaliev, former head of the Financial Police Syimyk Zhapykeev, former parliament member Baktybek Kalmamatov, and others. According to the CEC, the deadline for submitting candidacy applications is November 12, midnight (00:00). Next, the registration process for those running as candidates will take place.

articles.title: Norway follows Finland in barring Russian athletes from entering country over Ukraine war
articles.summary: Move by Norway ‘a further tightening’ of current rules Russians ‘have no business’ in Finland, says minister Norway’s government announced that it would prevent Russian and Belarusian professional athletes from coming to Norway to compete, hours after neighbouring Finland announced a similar move. The government said it intended to prevent athletes from these countries coming to Norway as long as the war in Ukraine continues.
articles.body: Norway’s government announced that it would prevent Russian and Belarusian professional athletes from coming to Norway to compete, hours after neighbouring Finland announced a similar move. The government said it intended to prevent athletes from these countries coming to Norway as long as the war in Ukraine continues. In a statement, it noted that while Norway already had strict rules for visas for Russian and Belarusian citizens, recent “relaxations introduced by international sports federations” meant that more athletes and support staff from the two countries may come to the Scandinavian nation to compete. In a statement, Astri Aas-Hansen, the minister of justice and public security, said: “Norway already has a restrictive visa practice for Russian and Belarusian citizens, but is now further tightening who is allowed to travel here.” To this end, the government said it would instruct immigration authorities and police to “to refuse entry to Russian and Belarusian professional athletes and accompanying support staff … if they come to Norway to take part in sporting competitions”. The changes would enter into force “shortly”, the government said. The statement said that Russian elite sport had close ties to Russian authorities and could therefore not be “viewed independently” from the war in Ukraine. Norway is preparing to host World Cup in cross-country skiing in December in the town of Trondheim, but this decision means that Russian and Belarusian athletes could be blocked from competing despite having been cleared by the International Ski and Snowboard Federation (FIS). FIS has permitted Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete under certain conditions, such as not displaying any country symbols and signing a declaration of neutrality. The Norwegian move follows a similar decision by Nordic neighbour Finland, which earlier on Thursday announced it would block visas for Russian athletes. Finland also said it will restrict entry for Russian athletes because of the war in Ukraine, potentially affecting a number of winter sports. The move follows a backlash in Finland to Russia being reinstated for the ice hockey world championships. “As long as Russia’s war of aggression continues, Russian athletes have no business in Finland,” said Elina Valtonen, the minister for foreign affairs. “Their entry into the country would be a threat to Finland’s international relations. The same is true of other short-term work under visas that is not essential to Finland’s national interests.” The Finnish foreign ministry said the measure would affect Russians competing under neutral status as well as those competing for national teams. Finland hosts a figure skating grand prix next week and a cross-country ski World Cup this month. Both sports allow Russians to compete as “neutral athletes”. One major event to be affected is the figure skating world championships in March. Russian skaters are expected to be among the top medal contenders. The International Skating Union (ISU) said it “has taken note of the statement today by the Finnish government related to Russian nationals entering the country and the possible consequential impact on sporting events, including the ISU figure skating world championships due to be held in Tampere, Finland, and is studying its implications”. “ISU believes that athletes should not be punished for the actions of their governments in a world where, sadly, many conflicts are ongoing.” The ISU added it was “seeking clarifications” from skating officials in Finland. The change takes effect from Monday, so should not affect this week’s NHL games in Helsinki between the Seattle Kraken and Carolina Hurricanes or scheduled ski World Cup slalom races in Levi on Saturday and Sunday. Finland is among a group of European teams to have vowed not to play against Russia at the ice hockey world championships. The men’s championships are scheduled for Germany, which is weighing up whether to go ahead with hosting. In the longer term, Finland is due to host the European track and field championships in 2030. World Athletics, the sport’s governing body, maintains a blanket ban on Russian participation, though that is facing a legal challenge.

articles.title: Opposition Ban Case Deepens as Court Hearings Become Increasingly Contentious
articles.summary: Georgia’s Constitutional Court is continuing to hear a high-stakes lawsuit seeking to ban five opposition parties, with this week’s proceedings marked by disputes over evidence, procedural rights and the timing of any potential ruling. Tensions inside the courtroom have also escalated, with two leading representatives of the Coalition for Change ordered to leave Wednesday’s hearing.
articles.body: Georgia’s Constitutional Court is continuing to hear a high-stakes lawsuit seeking to ban five opposition parties, with this week’s proceedings marked by disputes over evidence, procedural rights and the timing of any potential ruling. Tensions inside the courtroom have also escalated, with two leading representatives of the Coalition for Change ordered to leave Wednesday’s hearing. The case, brought by 88 members of the ruling Georgian Dream party, seeks to have five political groups declared unconstitutional and prohibited from operating: United National Movement; Coalition for Change, comprising Gvaramia, Melia, Girchi and Droa; Strong Georgia–Lelo, For the People, For Freedom!; the Federalist Party; and Gakharia Tor Georgia. The petition argues that the parties’ activities threaten Georgia’s constitutional order, independence, and territorial integrity. It also draws on the findings of a temporary parliamentary investigative commission established during the 11th convocation of Parliament. The opposition parties reject the allegations, describing the case as politically motivated and warning that a ban would remove a substantial part of the country’s political opposition. The Constitutional Court began examining the petition on October 21. The case is being heard by a seven-judge plenary panel, and a final ruling is expected by June 2027. The decision will be final and cannot be appealed within Georgia. Dispute over evidence Much of this week’s disagreement has centered on whether the court will properly examine the evidence presented by the plaintiffs before questioning the parties. On November 10, Levan Samushia, representing Strong Georgia–Lelo, submitted a motion requesting a separate evidentiary stage in the proceedings. Representatives of the other opposition parties supported the request, arguing that they needed an opportunity to examine and challenge the material on which Georgian Dream’s case was based. The court partially granted the motion, but its decision fell short of what the opposition had requested. Constitutional Court Chairman Revaz Nadaraia said the judges would not present every internet link cited in the petition or examine facts considered generally known and judicial decisions that had already entered into force. The court would instead assess the relevance of specific evidence if a party challenged it with a substantiated motion, or on its own initiative. Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Coalition for Change, said the ruling effectively removed an entire stage of judicial examination and deprived the respondents of an important opportunity to defend themselves. “What happened regarding the evidence is extremely problematic. I do not know how the court intends to get out of this situation. The entire stage of judicial examination has effectively been removed,” he said, describing the decision as incompatible with the requirements of the law. Grigol Gegelia, one of the leaders of Strong Georgia–Lelo, also questioned the strength of the case against the opposition parties. He said Georgian Dream had reacted nervously to the request to examine the evidence because it had little substantive material to support its allegations. “We will continue the process and fight until the end. We expect to liberate this country from Georgian Dream,” Gegelia said after the hearing. He argued that the lawsuit relied on what he described as absurd claims, despite potentially affecting the political rights of around one million voters. Court rejects request for a one-month delay Another procedural dispute arose after the Coalition for Change filed a motion on November 10 asking the court to ensure that, if it ruled in favor of banning the parties, the decision and its legal consequences would not take effect until at least one month after its announcement. Gvaramia said the request was intended to establish a single date for the implementation of any ban, including the cancellation of party registration. He stressed that submitting the motion did not mean the coalition expected the court to uphold the lawsuit or accepted any of the allegations against it. The request was also intended to preserve the possibility of seeking urgent interim measures from the European Court of Human Rights under Rule 39. This provision allows the Strasbourg court to indicate measures in exceptional circumstances where there is a risk of serious and irreparable harm. Constitutional Court Judge Eva Gotsiridze questioned the purpose of the motion, suggesting that it was designed to give the European Court time to intervene before a potential ban took effect. The Plenum subsequently rejected the request. Revaz Nadaraia said the Constitution and the Organic Law on the Constitutional Court did not provide for a separate procedural order committing the court in advance to delay enforcement. Any decision to postpone the legal effects of a ruling, he said, would have to be addressed in the final judgment itself. “The Plenum has ruled that the motion presented by the Coalition for Change, which is supported by all the respondent parties, shall not be granted. This decision is final,” Nadaraia said, describing the request as legally unfounded. Tensions escalate inside the courtroom The questioning stage has brought further confrontations between the parties. On November 11, judges questioned representatives of Georgian Dream, with several exchanges involving Archil Gorduladze, Chairman of the Parliament of Georgia’s Legal Affairs Committee, and opposition representatives. Judge Gotsiridze asked the plaintiffs whether they had evidence linking the opposition parties to violence. Gorduladze cited Murtaz Zodelava and Paata Burchuladze, both charged in connection with the events of October 4, 2025, when a group of activists attempted to storm the presidential palace. He said both men had links to the United National Movement. Gvaramia challenged the assertion, arguing that neither man was a member of the party. The exchange became heated, and Constitutional Court Chairman Revaz Nadaraia ordered Gvaramia to leave the courtroom, followed by Maia Kopaleishvili, another Coalition for Change representative and a former Constitutional Court judge. Kopaleishvili described her removal as a restriction on the defendants’ ability to participate in the proceedings. “This is a show of force,” she said as she left. The coalition subsequently sought permission for both representatives to return. Gorduladze, meanwhile, accused opposition representatives of trying to turn the proceedings into television debates rather than a legal examination of the case. “They know that their unconstitutional actions have no legal justification, and now they are trying to get by solely through demagoguery,” he said. He also criticized Gvaramia’s request concerning the timing of a potential ruling, calling it legally absurd. Gorduladze argued that opposition representatives resorted to what he described as “legal nonsense” when they lacked substantive arguments. Church figure questions whether bans can bring lasting results The proposed ban has also prompted comment beyond the political parties involved in the case. Metropolitan Nikoloz Pachuashvili of Akhalkalaki, Kumurdo and Kari said that preventing people from expressing their views could not produce meaningful or lasting results. Asked about the proceedings, he said the Church should speak the truth while avoiding political statements for which its members might lack the necessary expertise. He stressed, however, that this should not be interpreted as a reluctance to challenge the authorities. “Preventing someone from speaking through prohibition is not a solution aimed at long-term results. We cannot achieve meaningful results this way,” he said. The Metropolitan compared the situation to disagreements within the Church, where those expressing what clergy consider false teachings are generally answered through discussion rather than prevented from speaking. He added that responsibility for reducing political polarization rested primarily with the government, although opposition parties and individual politicians also had a role to play. Hearings to continue The Constitutional Court resumed proceedings on November 12, at time of going to press, with judges expected to question representatives of the opposition parties. Another hearing is scheduled for Friday, November 13. According to Nadaraia, the question-and-answer stage is expected to continue until November 17. The latest exchanges have highlighted the sharply different positions of the two sides. Georgian Dream maintains that the parties targeted by the petition threaten the constitutional order and that the proceedings are a legitimate defense of democracy. The opposition argues that the case is an attempt to eliminate political competitors and deprive voters of their chosen representatives. With the court yet to complete its questioning, the central issue remains unresolved: whether the evidence and arguments presented by the plaintiffs meet the constitutional threshold for banning political parties. The eventual ruling could have far-reaching consequences for political competition in Georgia. By Team GT

articles.title: Constitutional Court Ruling in the Veronica Dragalin Case: Provision That Led to the Vetting Process Not Being Approved Declared Unconstitutional
articles.summary: Judges and prosecutors who resigned after the legal 20-day deadline will be allowed to continue the vetting process if they request it. The Constitutional Court has ruled that a resignation submitted after this deadline can no longer automatically be treated as a failure to pass the integrity assessment.
articles.body: Judges and prosecutors who resigned after the legal 20-day deadline will be allowed to continue the vetting process if they request it. The Constitutional Court has ruled that a resignation submitted after this deadline can no longer automatically be treated as a failure to pass the integrity assessment. The ruling was issued on November 12, following the examination of a referral concerning the case of former Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office head Veronica Dragalin, Rupor.md reports. The Court declared the phrase “regardless of the reason given” in the Law on the External Evaluation of Judges and Prosecutors unconstitutional. Until now, the provision stipulated that individuals who resigned more than 20 days after receiving notification that their evaluation had begun were automatically considered to have failed the vetting process. Under the new procedure established by the Court, the evaluation will continue at the request of the person concerned, even if their resignation was submitted after the statutory deadline. These rules will apply until Parliament amends the legislation. The referral was examined in the context of a case before the Supreme Court of Justice challenging the evaluation of Veronica Dragalin. It was submitted by judges Stela Procopciuc, Ion Munteanu and Vladislav Gribincea, together with Vladimir Grosu, the lawyer representing the former head of the Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office. The Constitutional Court partially upheld the referral. The lawyer’s other requests, which challenged several additional provisions of the law, were declared inadmissible. Veronica Dragalin announced her resignation on February 19, 2025, and her mandate ended on March 4. In June, the evaluation commission ruled that she had failed the vetting process because she had resigned outside the deadline established by law. Later, on July 17, the Superior Council of Prosecutors approved the commission’s report and imposed a five-year ban on Dragalin holding the position of prosecutor or other public office. The ban is calculated from the date on which the decision becomes final. The Constitutional Court’s ruling is final, cannot be appealed and entered into force on the day it was issued. Parliament is to be notified so that the legislation can be brought into line with the decision. Two separate opinions were also expressed during the examination of the case.

articles.title: Albania's Prime Minister Rama meets Zelensky, urges Europe to open talks with Russia
articles.summary: Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Dublin on Thursday, a few hours after telling reporters that Europe had left its diplomacy on Russia to President Donald Trump.
articles.body: Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Dublin on Thursday, a few hours after telling reporters that Europe had left its diplomacy on Russia to President Donald Trump. Both men were in the Irish capital for a meeting of the European Political Community , a gathering of more than 50 European leaders chaired this year by Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin and European Council President António Costa. Speaking to reporters as he arrived, Rama said Europe had been right to send weapons to Ukraine but wrong to stop talking to Moscow. "I believe it was a big mistake to leave diplomacy in the hands of others and to focus only on military support for Ukraine, which is the right thing to do, without keeping a channel of dialogue open with Russia," he said. "Whether we like it or not, Russia is not going anywhere." Talks with Russia should not be left to Washington, Beijing or New Delhi, he said. "It's up to Europe to understand the mistake it has made." Rama said he was uneasy that Europe had relied on arms instead of diplomacy. But Albania is a small country, he added, and he was in no position to lecture the bigger ones. "Europe has outsourced its diplomacy to Donald Trump, and this is the result," he said. The price would keep going up, he warned, unless Europe opened talks with Russia while still backing Ukraine. Merkel and Qatari gas On Wednesday, in a speech at the Institute of International and European Affairs , a Dublin think tank, Rama said Europe had gone wrong "from day one" by giving up on diplomacy and betting on beating Russia outright. Europe had always leaned toward diplomacy, he said, and that decision changed its nature. He also asked why former German Chancellor Angela Merkel is blamed at home for buying cheap Russian gas. What would German voters have said, he wondered, if she had told them she was going to stop and pay more for gas from Qatar instead? Albania does not miss Russia, Rama said, and has no part to play in ending the war. "No one is asking Albania to solve anything, and no one can blame it when things go unresolved." He has said much the same before. In April, at the Delphi Economic Forum in Greece, he told Politico that cutting every channel with Russia was a "big strategic mistake" and that the longer Europe waited, the less say it would have in a settlement. In November 2025 he told the Austrian daily Die Presse that the EU should talk to Russia and stop outsourcing its foreign policy to Washington, because Russia is Europe's neighbor, not America's. Rama usually adds that Albania has no ties to Russia. Russian state media have picked up on his comments. TASS reported the Die Presse interview, and RIA Novosti the one with Politico. Who talks to Putin? Rama's remarks came as leaders in Dublin argued over who should speak for Europe if talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin ever take place. Rapporteur , a Brussels-based outlet, reported that Costa called for a "team effort" by Europe, the EU and NATO. Kaja Kallas, the EU's foreign policy chief, said the matter was settled when she and Costa were chosen for their jobs in 2024. Albania is an EU candidate and has signed on to the bloc's foreign policy positions, including sanctions on Russia. Rama's government wants to finish membership talks by the end of 2027.

articles.title: Constitutional Court assesses legality of dismissing teachers for immoral misconduct
articles.summary: Tengrinews.kz — In Kazakhstan, teachers may be dismissed for immoral misconduct deemed incompatible with continuing their teaching duties. The Constitutional Court considered whether this ground for dismissal is defined clearly enough in the Labor Code.
articles.body: Tengrinews.kz — In Kazakhstan, teachers may be dismissed for immoral misconduct deemed incompatible with continuing their teaching duties. The Constitutional Court considered whether this ground for dismissal is defined clearly enough in the Labor Code. The case was prompted by an appeal from a woman who had been dismissed under subparagraph 14 of paragraph 1 of Article 52 of the Labor Code for committing immoral misconduct incompatible with continuing her work. The decision to dismiss her was made by the school’s pedagogical ethics council. Disagreeing with the decision, the woman appealed to a conciliation commission and later to the courts. However, the court rulings in her case were left unchanged. The woman argued that the law does not provide clear characteristics or objective criteria for what constitutes immoral misconduct. In her view, this allows employers to interpret the provision too broadly and violates an employee’s right to work and judicial protection. Why the court did not require an exact list of misconduct The Constitutional Court noted that existing legislation already sets requirements for the moral conduct of employees performing educational duties. In particular, there are specific rules on pedagogical ethics and liability for violating them. “The concept of ‘immoral misconduct’ is inherently evaluative, so its meaning cannot be exhaustively defined through a closed list of actions. Assessing such misconduct requires taking into account the circumstances of the specific case, as well as the social, cultural and professional context,” the court said. What the Constitutional Court decided Following its review, the court concluded that the concept of “immoral misconduct” has sufficient legal certainty and allows the relevant provision to be applied while taking into account the circumstances of each individual case. The Constitutional Court also noted that the applicant had made use of the legal mechanisms available to protect her rights by appealing to the conciliation commission and the courts. As a result, the court did not find the challenged provision unconstitutional.

articles.summary: Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya said that Belarus’s political and military situation must be included in any Russia-Ukraine peace negotiations. She made the remarks on Nov. 12 at the European Political Community (EPC) Summit in Dublin, Ireland.
articles.body: Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya said that Belarus’s political and military situation must be included in any Russia-Ukraine peace negotiations. She made the remarks on Nov. 12 at the European Political Community (EPC) Summit in Dublin, Ireland. The EPC brings together leaders from across the European continent, including countries outside the European Union, with Russia and Belarus under Alexander Lukashenko excluded from the forum. Tsikhanouskaya represents Belarus as the "leader of the democratic forces." She is widely believed to have won the disputed 2020 presidential election. "Without a free and democratic Belarus , there will be no security, neither for Ukraine nor for European countries," Tsikhanouskaya said ahead of the summit's opening. "I really think that Belarus should be an issue in negotiations about peace in the region," Tsikhanouskaya said, before adding that "we have to demand withdrawal of Russian troops not only from Ukraine, but also from Belarus." Belarus under Lukashenko is considered by the West to be operating as a co-belligerent in Russia's war against Ukraine. Moscow has a heavy military presence in the country, used Belarus to launch the initial full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and has used Belarusian territory to launch various attacks in the years since then. Western governments have also tended to treat Russia and Belarus similarly, both in restricting their participation in international forums and in imposing sanctions on the two countries. Tsikhanouskaya sought to highlight the contributions of ordinary Belarusians in support of Ukraine, for example, by their volunteering for the Ukrainian armed forces. We have to "give all the opportunities to help Ukrainians win this war because the victory of Ukraine will shape not only their future, but the future of the whole of Europe," Tsikhanouskaya said.

Bosnian Court Convicts Three of Wartime Abuses of Civilian Prisoners
articles.summary: The state court handed down 41 years of prison time to three defendants for committing war crimes against detained civilians in Bosanski Novi in 1992.
articles.body: The Bosnian state court on Thursday sentenced Mira Bosancic to 17 years in prison, and Simo Licina and Zarko Kalinic to 12 years each, for crimes against civilians who were detained in the fire station building in Bosanski Novi during the Bosnian war in ​​1992. In the first-instance verdict, the court found Bosancic, Licina and Kalinic guilty of committing crimes against humanity – persecution by murder, enforced disappearance and physical abuse. They committed the crimes while serving as military policemen with the Bosnian Serb Army’s Light Novograd Brigade. “The judging panel has determined that during the relevant period, a widespread and systematic attack by the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, now Republika Srpska, took place,” presiding judge Halil Lagumdzija said. Bosancic was found guilty on three counts of participating in the beating of detained civilians in the basement of the fire station building, as well seizing several people who have been missing ever since. Licina and Kalinic were found guilty of tying up and stripping a prisoner, cutting him with a knife and then pouring salt on him. The prisoner died of his injuries. “His body was taken away and has not been found to this day,” said Lagumdzija. However, the judges found that it had not been proven that Bosancic participated in the forced disappearance of two civilians and the killing of another. Due to lack of evidence, the defendants were acquitted of beating and taking away two men. Four other defendants in the trial – Nedjeljko Pilipovic and Bogdan, Zarko and Jovan Grab – were acquitted of all charges.

articles.title: Billions meant for science misused: SAC audit reveals budget irregularities
articles.summary: Kazakhstan’s Supreme Audit Chamber has reviewed government spending on science, presenting its findings at a meeting of the Kurultai, the nation’s recently inaugurated unicameral parliament, on Nov. 11, 2026. Of 141 completed projects, only 38, or 27%, generated consistent sales over a three-year period.
articles.body: Kazakhstan’s Supreme Audit Chamber has reviewed government spending on science, presenting its findings at a meeting of the Kurultai , the nation’s recently inaugurated unicameral parliament, on Nov. 11, 2026. Of 141 completed projects, only 38, or 27%, generated consistent sales over a three-year period. Another 103 projects, accounting for 22 billion tenge, failed to achieve their planned production or sales targets. The Chamber estimated the total value of financial irregularities and inefficient spending in the sector at 98 billion tenge (about $217 million). Auditors noted that between 2022 and 2025, government funding for science more than doubled, rising from 122 billion to 262 billion tenge. During this period, the National Academy of Sciences was established, universities and research institutions began upgrading their equipment, and new support measures for young scientists were introduced. In 2026, the development of science and innovation was enshrined in the Constitution as a strategic priority. However, science still accounts for just 0.16% of gross domestic product (GDP), well below the 1% target. According to Kursiv.media’s calculations, the gap is approximately sixfold. Meanwhile, the government’s share of total science funding has increased from 55% to 82%. Auditors attributed this trend to weak demand from businesses for research and development (R&D). Between 2021 and 2025, Kazakhstan had four policy documents governing the development of science. Three were discontinued before their scheduled expiration dates, and their targets were subsequently revised downward. For example, the R&D spending target as a share of GDP was initially set at 2% but was later reduced to 0.5%. The planned increase in the number of researchers was cut from 50% to 7%, while the target for private-sector funding was lowered from 50% to 32%. For 2025–2027, the government approved seven priority areas and 153 specific research topics. According to auditors, the list is so broad that almost any research project could qualify as a priority. Project assignments are also often vaguely worded, lacking clearly defined expected outcomes, verification criteria and implementation plans. Of the 393 projects commissioned for 2023–2025, 149, worth a combined 67 billion tenge, were not completed. Auditors also raised concerns about funding arrangements. A total of 62 billion tenge was allocated to 79 projects without detailed expenditure breakdowns. «Even if the final report is rejected, most of the funding remains with the contractor: 96% to 98% of a project’s total value is paid out before the final evaluation,» the Chamber said. Alikhan Smailov , chairman of the Supreme Audit Chamber, said 176 projects worth 16 billion tenge had failed to achieve their intended outcomes. Although monitoring identified these shortcomings, no corrective measures were taken. In 2025, monitoring covered more than 2,000 projects and uncovered violations totaling over 3 billion tenge. However, according to Smailov, the national scientific councils merely «took note of the information» without taking further action. Competitive selection procedures for 2025 projects were delayed by as much as 208 days, disrupting the entire research cycle. The submission of expert assessments to scientific councils was also delayed by up to 93 days. Additionally, recommendations by economic experts to reduce funding for 545 projects by approximately 12 billion tenge were not followed. Auditors also identified potential conflicts of interest among scientific council members. Of the 225 members, 84 participated in research teams working on 127 projects worth a combined 52 billion tenge. Another 27 council members served as scientific supervisors for these projects. According to Smailov, scientific performance is often assessed using formal indicators, including publications, intellectual property documents and records of implementation. However, these indicators do not necessarily demonstrate that a project has produced a tangible technological or industrial result. Projects typically conclude with a final report, but the subsequent use of their findings is not monitored. The audit found that no agreements had been signed for the use of 60 patents included in the sample. Commercialization also remains a challenge. According to the Science Fund, the commercialization rate stands at 44%. However, when calculated on a comparable basis for the reporting year, the figure falls to 16%. The mechanism requiring subsoil users to allocate 1% of their revenue to scientific research has also failed to become an effective funding instrument. Auditors found that compliance with these obligations is poorly monitored and that some of the funds received have been diverted from research activities into bank deposits, securities and repurchase agreements (repos). The audit identified 51 billion tenge in financial irregularities and another 47 billion tenge in inefficient planning and use of funds. Materials concerning 36 violations have been submitted for administrative proceedings, while cases involving three incidents have been referred to law enforcement agencies. The Chamber has also issued recommendations and directives to the government and relevant state agencies.

articles.title: Konakovic: Dodik Is Gathering Teams for Secession Again, Buying the Favor of People Close to Trump with Russian Money
articles.summary: At today’s press conference, Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Elmedin Konaković, said Milorad Dodik initiated activities aimed at the secession of Republika Srpska a few weeks ago. He also made serious accusations about financing lobbying in the United States, warned future coalition partners not to hand over key state institutions to the SNSD, […] The post Konakovic: Dodik Is Gathering Teams for Secession…
articles.body: At today’s press conference, Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Elmedin Konaković, said Milorad Dodik initiated activities aimed at the secession of Republika Srpska a few weeks ago. He also made serious accusations about financing lobbying in the United States, warned future coalition partners not to hand over key state institutions to the SNSD, and spoke about issuing diplomatic passports. Konaković made a statement that Dodik has recently renewed concrete activities linked with secessionist plans, stating that information was verified within intelligence circles. “A few weeks ago, Dodik restarted formal activities on secession. He has started gathering working groups, teams, and people. We checked that information within intelligence circles and received confirmations,” said Konaković. According to his assessment, the shift of political circumstances in Serbia and problems faced by Dodik’s lobbyists in the US could affect the further development of those plans. “It seems to me that he will slowly freeze that idea, considering that he suffered a crash in the elections in Serbia,” he stated. He emphasized that he considers Dodik’s actions more dangerous than before. “Dodik has been more radical in the last two years than ever. This is no longer just a narrative,” he warned. During the conference, Konaković did not present documents that would allow independent verification of his claims about the re-gathering of secessionist teams. Warning to SDA: “You must not give Dodik four ministers” Speaking about the formation of the new government, Konaković called on the election winners to start fulfilling promises as soon as possible, and to especially take heed of the distribution of positions. “We are not interested in power; we are interested in the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We will help everyone who has good intentions to establish a functional government as soon as possible,” he stated. He especially warned about the possibility of the SNSD getting four ministerial positions in the Council of Ministers of BiH. “I see that we already have some signs of Dodik’s madness in his demands. The Constitutional Court once again, the transfer of competencies once again. I know that this is his game, so that he can set the bar high, and then be, supposedly, satisfied with four ministers at the Council of Ministers, which must not happen.” He stated that ceding such positions would be a serious mistake of the future coalition. “It is unnatural for the SNSD to have four ministers anytime and anywhere, and our side to have three. I appeal that this is the demand number one and that they do not play with that.” “We must not, for the life of us, surrender the Ministry of Foreign Affairs,” he said, warning that Dodik’s cadres could use the diplomatic network to promote secessionist goals. “I would give that to Dodik. This has nothing to do with ethnicity. Crnadak was here before; there were people from the ranks of the Serb people who did their job correctly.” Konaković also made an assessment that SDA is stalling negotiations so that the SDP, after the formation of the House of Peoples, becomes an indispensable partner in the new government. One of the sharpest parts of the conference referred to Dodik’s lobbying in the US and the Continental Strategy Campaign, which is business-connected to people in Donald Trump’s close circles. Asked whether he expects that announced US investigations could include lobbying for Republika Srpska, Konaković replied: “I expect it. We saw the indications immediately after elections. Allow me to gloat a bit on that topic. I think we showed them how processes are run.” He claimed that institutions of BiH tracked lobbyist activities and delivered relevant information to the US institutions. “We delivered the information to the State Department, Congress, and Senate. These will certainly be interested in cleaning that up to the end.” He then made particularly serious accusations about the origin of money which was used to finance the lobbying. “The point is that part of that lobbying was paid for with Putin’s money. Effectively, he was buying the favor of people close to President Trump with Russian money, not President Trump or his administration,” Konaković asserted,” Konaković confirmed. During the conference, he did not present financial evidence that would confirm the money originated from the Russian president. “That is lobbying for Russian interests. That’s the biggest problem of US lobbyists. They were lobbying for a Russian mercenary in Europe,” he said. He mentioned former Illinois Governor Rod Blagojevich and the former US National Security Advisor Michael Flynn, criticizing their engagements connected to Dodik. “Now that is going to blow up in Dodik’s face, as our people say, as he deserved,” he concluded.
